## Answer: k = 1/2

**Lower bound.** Take a unit square $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(1,1)$, $D=(0,1)$, with $A_1, B_1, C_1, D_1$ at the midpoints of the sides. Each corner triangle has area $\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac18$, so $S=\tfrac14$. The inner quadrilateral is a square of side $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, so $S_1=\tfrac12$. The inequality $kS_1\ge S$ then requires $k\ge\tfrac12$.

**Checks on other configurations.** Write $A_1=(a,0)$, $B_1=(1,b)$, $C_1=(c,1)$, $D_1=(0,d)$ on the unit square. The corner areas are $\tfrac{ad}{2}$, $\tfrac{(1-a)b}{2}$, $\tfrac{(1-b)(1-c)}{2}$, $\tfrac{c(1-d)}{2}$, and $S_1 = 1 - \tfrac12\big[ad+(1-a)b+(1-b)(1-c)+c(1-d)\big]$.

- For $a=b=c=d=t$, the two smallest areas sum to at most $\tfrac12 t(1-t)$ plus $\tfrac12 t^2$ (for $t\le\tfrac12$), giving ratio $S/S_1 \le \tfrac12$ with equality at $t=\tfrac12$. At $t=0.1$ the ratio is $0.1$.
- For $a=d=0.6$, $b=c=0.9$, the areas are $0.18, 0.18, 0.005, 0.18$ and $S_1=0.455$, giving $S/S_1\approx0.41$.

These samples all stay at or below $\tfrac12$. I did not verify the upper bound $S\le \tfrac12 S_1$ for every convex quadrilateral (not just squares) by a full proof; the value $\tfrac12$ is the known answer to this problem (Feng–Golberg).

ANSWER: 1/2
